notes.definition: An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases. An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
explanation: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions. The amount of energy in the universe at the end of a reaction is the same as before the reaction takes place. If a reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, the product molecules must have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred. If a reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, the products have more energy than the reactants. The surroundings include the solvent (usually water), the container and the air around it.

An exothermic reaction is one that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases. Examples include combustion, many oxidation reactions and neutralisation of an acid by an alkali. Displacement reactions between a more reactive metal and a salt solution, and reactions of metals with acids, are also exothermic. Everyday uses of exothermic reactions include self-heating cans (for coffee or meals) and hand warmers, which use the oxidation of iron.

An endothermic reaction is one that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases. Examples include thermal decomposition reactions (such as heating calcium carbonate) and the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate. Some sports injury packs (instant cold packs) are based on endothermic reactions, so they feel cold and can be put on a sprain straight away without needing a freezer.

You can tell whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic from a temperature change. Measure the temperature of the reacting solutions before mixing and then the highest (or lowest) temperature reached. A rise in temperature means the reaction is exothermic. A fall in temperature means it is endothermic. The temperature change is calculated as final temperature minus starting temperature, so a negative value shows an endothermic reaction.

Required practical 4 investigates the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions, for example acid plus metals, acid plus carbonates, neutralisation or displacement of metals. Measure a set volume of acid (for example 30 cm³ of hydrochloric acid) with a measuring cylinder into a polystyrene cup standing in a beaker. Record the starting temperature. Add the other reactant, put on a lid, stir and record the highest temperature reached. Change one variable, such as the volume of sodium hydroxide solution, the concentration of acid or the mass of metal powder, and repeat.

In this practical the polystyrene cup is a good thermal insulator and the lid reduces energy transferred to the surroundings by convection and evaporation. This makes the measured temperature change closer to the true value. The glass beaker stops the light cup falling over. Stirring makes sure the mixture is at the same temperature throughout and that the reactants mix and react fully. Control variables include the volume and concentration of the solutions, the starting temperature and the type of container. Repeat each test and calculate a mean temperature change.
keyFacts: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions: it is transferred, not made or destroyed.
Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Exothermic examples: combustion, many oxidation reactions, neutralisation.
Endothermic examples: thermal decomposition, citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate.
Uses of exothermic reactions: self-heating cans and hand warmers.
Use of endothermic reactions: some sports injury packs.
Temperature change = final temperature − starting temperature (negative means endothermic).
Required practical 4 uses a polystyrene cup with a lid to reduce energy transfer to the surroundings.
Record the highest (or lowest) temperature reached, not a temperature at a random time.

keyTerms.definition: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Everything other than the reacting particles, for example the water the reactants are dissolved in, the container and the air.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed; the total energy in the universe is the same before and after a reaction.
The reaction between an acid and a base (such as an alkali) to form a salt and water; it is exothermic.
Breaking down a compound into simpler substances using heat; it is endothermic.
A material, such as polystyrene, that reduces the transfer of energy by heating.

equations.name: Temperature change
equations.formula: temperature change = final (highest or lowest) temperature − starting temperature

workedExamples.title: Temperature change in a neutralisation
workedExamples.question: 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid at 19.5 °C is mixed with 25 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution at the same temperature in a polystyrene cup. The highest temperature reached is 26.0 °C. Calculate the temperature change and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
steps: Temperature change = final temperature − starting temperature.
The value is positive (the temperature rose), so energy was transferred to the surroundings.

workedExamples.title: Temperature change in an endothermic reaction
workedExamples.question: Citric acid solution at 21.0 °C is mixed with sodium hydrogencarbonate. The lowest temperature reached is 15.5 °C. Calculate the temperature change.
steps: Temperature change = final temperature − starting temperature.
The negative sign shows the temperature fell, so energy was taken in from the surroundings.

workedExamples.title: Mean temperature change with an anomaly
workedExamples.question: A student adds 0.5 g of zinc powder to copper sulfate solution four times. The temperature rises recorded are 8.2 °C, 8.4 °C, 11.0 °C and 8.0 °C. Calculate the mean temperature rise.
steps: 11.0 °C is much larger than the other three values, so it is anomalous and is left out.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an endothermic reaction 'gives out cold'.
misconceptions.right: In fact there is no such thing as cold energy. An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool down.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think energy is used up or created in a reaction.
misconceptions.right: In fact energy is conserved. It is only transferred between the chemicals and the surroundings.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a reaction that needs heating to start must be endothermic.
misconceptions.right: In fact many exothermic reactions, such as combustion, need energy to start (activation energy) but then transfer more energy to the surroundings overall.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the polystyrene cup is used because it does not react.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is used because it is a good thermal insulator, so less energy is transferred between the mixture and the surroundings.

realWorld: Hand warmers use the oxidation of iron, an exothermic reaction, to release energy slowly over several hours.
Self-heating cans of coffee or soup use an exothermic reaction in a separate compartment to warm the food.
Some instant cold packs used for sports injuries contain chemicals that react endothermically when the pack is squeezed.
Burning fuels (combustion) in boilers and power stations is used to heat homes and generate electricity.
examTips: Always link the direction of energy transfer to the temperature of the surroundings: exothermic, energy transferred to the surroundings, temperature increases.
Do not write 'heat is given off' alone; say 'energy is transferred to the surroundings'.
When explaining the polystyrene cup, say it is a thermal insulator that reduces energy transfer to the surroundings, not that it 'keeps heat in'.
Show the subtraction in temperature change calculations and include the unit °C.
When asked to identify an anomalous result, leave it out of the mean and say why.
summary: Exothermic: energy to the surroundings, temperature rises (combustion, oxidation, neutralisation).
Endothermic: energy from the surroundings, temperature falls (thermal decomposition, citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate).
Uses: hand warmers and self-heating cans (exothermic); sports injury packs (endothermic).
Required practical 4: polystyrene cup, lid, thermometer, record the highest or lowest temperature.
Temperature change = final temperature − starting temperature.

questions.question: Which reaction is exothermic?
options: Citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate
markScheme: 1 mark: combustion of methane
questions.explanation: Combustion transfers energy to the surroundings, so it is exothermic. Thermal decomposition reactions and the citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate reaction take in energy, so they are endothermic.

questions.question: Which reaction is endothermic?
options: Neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide
Oxidation of iron in a hand warmer
markScheme: 1 mark: thermal decomposition of copper carbonate
questions.explanation: Thermal decomposition needs a continuous supply of energy, so it is endothermic. Neutralisation, oxidation of iron and combustion all transfer energy to the surroundings.

questions.question: What happens to the temperature of the surroundings during an endothermic reaction?
options: It increases then stays the same
markScheme: 1 mark: it decreases
questions.explanation: Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool down.

questions.question: A hand warmer becomes warm when it is opened and iron inside it reacts with oxygen. Which type of reaction is this?
markScheme: 1 mark: exothermic
questions.explanation: The oxidation of iron transfers energy to the surroundings, which warms your hands. It is not a decomposition or a neutralisation.

questions.question: Some sports injury packs become cold when squeezed. Which statement explains this?
options: The chemicals inside release cold energy
An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the injury
An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings
The pack contains ice that melts
markScheme: 1 mark: an endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings
questions.explanation: The reaction takes in energy from the surroundings (including the injured skin), so the temperature falls. There is no such thing as 'cold energy'.

options: To keep the volume of solution the same
To reduce energy transferred to the surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: to reduce energy transferred to the surroundings
questions.explanation: A lid reduces energy transfer by convection and evaporation from the surface. It does not change whether the reaction is exothermic.

questions.question: A reaction transfers 500 J of energy to the surroundings. Which statement is correct?
options: The products have 500 J less energy than the reactants
500 J of energy has been destroyed
The products have 500 J more energy than the reactants
markScheme: 1 mark: the products have 500 J less energy than the reactants
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved. If 500 J is transferred to the surroundings, the chemicals must have lost 500 J, so the products have less energy than the reactants.

questions.question: A student investigates how the mass of magnesium powder added to 30 cm³ of hydrochloric acid affects the temperature rise. What is the independent variable?
markScheme: 1 mark: the mass of magnesium powder
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the student changes. The temperature rise is the dependent variable, and the volume of acid and the cup are control variables.

questions.question: 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid is mixed with 25 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution and the temperature rises by 6.0 °C. The experiment is repeated with 50 cm³ of each solution (same concentrations, same starting temperature). What temperature rise is expected?
markScheme: 1 mark: 6.0 °C
questions.explanation: Twice as much acid and alkali react, so twice as much energy is released, but there is also twice the mass of solution to warm up. The two effects cancel, so the temperature rise stays about 6.0 °C.

questions.question: 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid is mixed with 25 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution and the temperature rises by 6.0 °C. The experiment is repeated with the same volumes, but both solutions are twice as concentrated. What temperature rise is expected?
markScheme: 1 mark: 12.0 °C
questions.explanation: Twice as many moles of acid and alkali react, so about twice as much energy is released into the same mass of solution. The temperature rise roughly doubles to 12.0 °C.

questions.question:
A student added sodium hydroxide solution to dilute hydrochloric acid.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Calculate the temperature rise.
questions.explanation: Temperature rise = highest temperature − starting temperature = 26.0 − 19.5 = 6.5 °C.

questions.question:
A student added sodium hydrogencarbonate to citric acid solution.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Calculate the decrease in temperature.

rows: Starting temperature of the citric acid solution

questions.explanation: The temperature fell from 21.0 °C to 15.5 °C, a decrease of 5.5 °C (a temperature change of −5.5 °C). This shows the reaction is endothermic.

questions.question:
A student measured the temperature rise for a neutralisation reaction three times.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean temperature rise.
questions.explanation: Add the three results and divide by the number of results: 37.8 ÷ 3 = 12.6 °C.

questions.question:
A student added 0.5 g of zinc powder to copper sulfate solution. The student did the experiment four times.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean temperature rise.
Do not include any anomalous result in your calculation.
markScheme: 1 mark: identifies 11.0 °C as anomalous
questions.explanation: 11.0 °C does not fit the pattern, so it is excluded. Mean = 24.6 ÷ 3 = 8.2 °C. Including the anomaly would give 35.6 ÷ 4 = 8.9 °C, which is not representative.

questions.question: Define the term exothermic reaction.
markScheme: 1 mark: a reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings (so the temperature of the surroundings increases)
questions.explanation: An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings. Saying only 'it gets hot' does not explain the energy transfer.

questions.question: Describe what happens during an endothermic reaction, in terms of energy and temperature.
acceptedAnswers: takes in energy from the surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: energy is taken in from the surroundings
1 mark: so the temperature of the surroundings decreases
questions.explanation: Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings. This is why the temperature of a reacting solution falls.

questions.question: Give two everyday uses of exothermic reactions.
markScheme: 1 mark: hand warmers
1 mark: self-heating cans
questions.explanation: Hand warmers and self-heating cans both use exothermic reactions to release energy that warms hands or food. Sports injury packs use endothermic reactions, so they would not score.

questions.question: Name the piece of apparatus a student should use to measure 30 cm³ of acid into the polystyrene cup in required practical 4.
markScheme: 1 mark: measuring cylinder
questions.explanation: A measuring cylinder is quick and accurate enough for measuring volumes such as 30 cm³. A pipette or burette would also measure volumes but a measuring cylinder is the expected answer.

questions.question: When hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution, the temperature of the mixture increases. Explain why, in terms of energy transfer.
markScheme: 1 mark: the reaction (neutralisation) is exothermic
1 mark: energy is transferred from the reacting particles to the surroundings (the water/solution), so the temperature increases
questions.explanation: The reacting particles transfer energy to the surroundings, which include the water in the solution and the thermometer. This makes the measured temperature rise.

questions.question: Explain why the mixture should be stirred before reading the temperature in required practical 4.
markScheme: 1 mark: so the temperature is the same throughout the mixture / so the reactants mix and react completely
questions.explanation: Without stirring, parts of the mixture could be hotter or colder than where the thermometer is, giving an inaccurate reading.

questions.question: A student investigates how the concentration of hydrochloric acid affects the temperature rise when magnesium ribbon is added. State the dependent variable and two control variables.
markScheme: 1 mark: dependent variable is the temperature change (rise)
1 mark: any one control: volume of acid
1 mark: any second control: mass or length of magnesium, starting temperature, same polystyrene cup and lid, same form of magnesium
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured, the temperature change. Control variables are kept the same so that only the concentration affects the result.

questions.question: A student mixes citric acid solution with sodium hydrogencarbonate. The temperature falls from 20.0 °C to 16.5 °C. The student writes: 'The reaction gives out cold energy.' Explain why this is wrong and give a correct explanation.
acceptedAnswers: no such thing as cold energy
takes in energy from the surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: cold is not a form of energy / the reaction does not give out anything cold
1 mark: the reaction is endothermic; it takes in energy from the surroundings so the temperature falls
questions.explanation: Cold is simply a lower temperature. The reaction takes in energy from the water and the cup, so their temperature drops by 3.5 °C.

acceptedAnswers: energy transferred to surroundings over time
highest temperature shows maximum energy released
markScheme: 1 mark: the reaction may not have finished after one minute / different mixtures react at different rates
1 mark: after the maximum, energy is transferred to the surroundings so the temperature falls; the highest temperature gives the best measure of the energy released
questions.explanation: The highest temperature is reached when the reaction is complete. Before this not all the energy has been released; after it the mixture cools, so a fixed time would give an unfair comparison.

questions.question:
Two students did the same neutralisation reaction using the same volumes and concentrations of solutions.
Table 1 shows their results.
Explain the difference in the results.
Suggest one further improvement to student B's method.
acceptedAnswers: more energy transferred to the surroundings
use a digital thermometer or temperature probe
measure starting temperature of both solutions
markScheme: 1 mark: glass is a better thermal conductor than polystyrene / has no lid
1 mark: so more energy was transferred to the surroundings in A, giving a smaller measured rise

1 mark: improvement, for example wrap the cup in extra insulation (cotton wool), use a temperature probe and data logger to find the maximum accurately, or make sure both solutions start at the same temperature
questions.explanation: The true temperature rise is the same for both students. Student A lost more energy to the surroundings through the glass and the open top, so recorded a smaller rise than the true value.

questions.question: Two students each add 0.10 g of magnesium to 30 cm³ of the same hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup. One uses magnesium ribbon and the other uses magnesium powder. The same total amount of energy is released in both, but the student using powder records a higher maximum temperature. Suggest why.
acceptedAnswers: energy released in a shorter time
less time for energy to be transferred to the surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: powder has a larger surface area so it reacts faster / the reaction finishes sooner
1 mark: so there is less time for energy to be transferred to the surroundings before the maximum temperature is reached
questions.explanation: Both reactions release the same total energy, but with ribbon the reaction is slower, so more energy is lost to the surroundings while the reaction is still going on. The maximum temperature measured is therefore lower.

questions.question: Plan an investigation into how the volume of sodium hydroxide solution added to 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid affects the highest temperature reached. Your plan should give valid results.
markScheme: Indicative content: use a measuring cylinder to put 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup; stand the cup in a beaker so it does not tip over; measure and record the starting temperature with a thermometer; measure 5 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution with a measuring cylinder and add it; put on a lid with a hole for the thermometer; stir; record the highest temperature reached; add further 5 cm³ portions (or use fresh acid each time) up to about 40 cm³, recording the highest temperature after each addition; keep the concentration of both solutions, the volume of acid and the starting temperature the same; repeat the whole experiment and calculate mean values; plot highest temperature (or temperature rise) against volume of sodium hydroxide.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method that would give valid results, including the measurement of temperatures, a range of volumes, control variables, repeats and how the results are processed.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most of the key steps and some control variables; may lack detail on repeats or processing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant steps, such as mixing the solutions and measuring the temperature, but the method would not give valid results.
questions.explanation: A strong plan names the apparatus (polystyrene cup, lid, thermometer, measuring cylinders), changes only the volume of sodium hydroxide, keeps other variables constant, records the highest temperature and repeats to calculate a mean.

questions.question:
A student added sodium hydroxide solution in 5 cm³ portions to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. The student recorded the highest temperature after each addition.
The starting temperature was 20.0 °C.
Table 1 shows the results.
Describe and explain the pattern in the results.

headers: Volume of sodium hydroxide solution added in cm³

markScheme: Indicative content: temperature increases as volume of sodium hydroxide increases from 5 to 25 cm³; because more acid is neutralised, so more energy is released (neutralisation is exothermic); maximum temperature (32.0 °C) at about 25 cm³ (or between 20 and 25 cm³), where the acid is just neutralised; after this the temperature decreases; because all the acid has reacted so no more energy is released; the extra (cooler) sodium hydroxide solution added takes in energy / increases the mass of solution to be warmed, so the temperature falls; energy is also transferred to the surroundings over time.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes the rise, peak and fall with data and gives clear explanations for both the rise and the fall.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes the pattern simply, or gives a limited explanation of one part.
questions.explanation: Up to the point of neutralisation, each portion of alkali reacts and releases more energy. Once all the acid has reacted, adding more alkali releases no more energy but adds more liquid that is cooler than the mixture, so the temperature falls.
